design_detail: Quantitative review (the authors call it an effect-size analysis, and a meta-analysis where a test was used in more than one study) of 15 cross-sectional studies published 1987–2002 that compared people meeting DSM-III-R or DSM-IV criteria for cocaine abuse or dependence with healthy control groups on neuropsychological tests. Cohen's d was computed for each test variable; where several studies used the same variable, the mean and standard deviation of their ds were reported, with no weighting, confidence intervals or heterogeneity statistics described. Table 2 ranks 140 test variables by size, 93 of them from a single study (editors' count). Cohen's U2 is reported as an index of how well each test separates the groups. No protocol, appraisal of study quality, moderator analysis or publication-bias assessment.
can_establish: How large the group differences were on individual neuropsychological tests in a small set of cross-sectional studies (15 samples, 1987–2002) of people meeting criteria for cocaine abuse or dependence, and which tests had been used often enough to be summarized across studies.
cannot_establish: That cocaine caused the differences (no pre-use baseline, control groups' education and IQ not reported, concurrent alcohol abuse allowed), how precise any summary is (no weighting or confidence intervals, most rows from one study), whether differences persist or recover with abstinence (0 to 1075.5 days, not analysed), or, for several rows, whether the cocaine group did worse or better (the sign convention is not stated).

sample.recruitment: Search of PsycINFO and Medline for published English-language articles, publication years 1987–2002; keywords cocaine combined with memory, executive function, manual dexterity, cognition, attention, neurocognitive and neuropsychological; search date not reported (p. 192). The review does not describe how the primary samples were recruited; the titles of the included studies refer to outpatients, abstinent or withdrawn samples, and one sample with current use (pp. 202–204).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: published 1987–2002 (1987 chosen because cocaine dependence entered DSM-III-R that year); statistics convertible to d (means and SDs, F, t); participants meeting DSM-III-R or DSM-IV criteria for cocaine abuse or dependence; a matched healthy control group. Excluded: studies reporting only significance levels. Samples with concurrent alcohol abuse (but not dependence) were allowed (p. 192); the Discussion adds that studies of people with concurrent alcohol dependence were excluded (p. 201). Where a study tested people more than once, only the first occasion was used (p. 193).
sample.demographics: Cocaine groups only (Table 1, p. 193): study mean ages median 34 (range 26–40; 15 studies); men median 95%, mean 87% (range 53–100); education mean 12.2 years (SD 2.2; range of study means 5.4–14.1); white median 40% (12 studies); African-American median 75% (9 studies); Beck Depression Inventory median 10.4 (4 studies). Sample sizes: cocaine groups median 30 (range 16–61); control groups median 27 (range 16–138). No demographic data are given for the control groups.
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level. The numbers of records found, screened and excluded are not reported.
sample.selection_effects: Two databases, published English-language articles only, no reference-list or grey-literature search and no record flow, so the completeness of the 15 studies cannot be judged. Samples were small, mostly men and, where reported, mostly African-American, with about 12 years of education; the required matching of controls is not documented by any control-group data. Titles of included studies indicate groups with alcohol dependence (Robinson, Heaton & O'Malley, 1999), crack-cocaine-and-alcohol dependence (Di Sclafani et al., 2002) and polydrug use (Roselli & Ardila, 1996, as spelled in the reference list); which subgroups entered the analysis is not stated.

exposure.measurement: DSM-III-R or DSM-IV diagnosis of cocaine abuse or dependence as an inclusion criterion; how the primary studies made the diagnosis is not described. Amount and duration of use as reported by the primary studies; the authors note that several studies gave no amount or duration and that some reported only more than six months of use or more than 4 g a week (p. 200).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Duration of use (10 studies): median 77.3 months, mean 85.2 (SD 49.3), range of study means 8.5–169.0. Amount (5 studies): median 4.0 g/week, mean 6.1 (SD 4.4), range 2.3–12.7 (Table 1, p. 193). Route: mostly smoked freebase or crack, some intravenous or intranasal, not quantified (p. 201).
exposure.polysubstance: Concurrent DSM alcohol abuse (not dependence) was allowed to keep the findings generalizable; several samples included people using caffeine, nicotine and alcohol. The authors state that most people who use cocaine also drink, that the differences could be at least partly due to alcohol, and that combined cocaine and alcohol effects were beyond their scope (pp. 192, 201). Other drug use is not described, and no analysis separates samples with and without alcohol abuse.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Reported by 11 studies: median 23.6 days, mean 128.7 (SD 317.0), range 0–1075.5 days (Table 1, p. 193). The authors raise the question of acute intoxication versus abstinence effects (p. 200). How abstinence was verified is not described.

comparison.controls: Healthy control groups of the primary studies: 586 people by the text, in 15 samples (median 27, range 16–138); recruitment and screening of controls not described.
comparison.matching: A matched control group was an inclusion criterion, but no control-group age, sex, education or IQ is reported, so the matching cannot be checked.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No study had a pre-use cognitive baseline, and premorbid IQ or education is not compared. Table 2 shows differences of similar size on measures usually taken to reflect prior verbal ability or schooling (WAIS-R Vocabulary −0.95; WAIS Full Scale IQ −0.66 and Verbal IQ −0.62; Shipley-Hartford vocabulary −0.54; WRMT Word Attack −0.41; each from one study), which suggests that in some samples the groups differed in prior ability or education (editors' interpretation).

outcomes.instruments: Standard neuropsychological tests and batteries: WAIS and WAIS-R subtests and IQ scores, WMS and WMS-R, Trail Making Parts A and B, Stroop variants, Wisconsin Card Sorting Test, Booklet Categories Test, Rey-Osterrieth Complex Figure, CVLT, RAVLT, Benton Visual Retention Test, COWAT and other fluency tasks, Benton Multilingual Aphasia Examination (abbreviated), Boston Naming Test, finger tapping, grooved pegboard, MicroCog and CALCAP computerized batteries, PASAT, Speech Sounds Perception, Rhythm and Tactual Performance tests, Shipley-Hartford, Porteus Maze, Hooper Visual Organization Test (Table 2, pp. 195–198).
outcomes.validity_norms: Group comparisons only. No comparison with published norms, except the primary authors' remark, reported by the review, that controls scored low on the Speech Sounds Perception Test against norms (p. 199). U2 is a transformation of d under assumed normal distributions, not an observed classification rate: every printed U2 equals Φ(|d|/2) to within 0.01 (editors' check of all 140 rows).
outcomes.operationalization: The words deficit and impairment mean a group difference expressed as d (difference between group means in pooled standard deviation units). Test variables are ranked by absolute size and those above the median of 0.35 are read as the most affected functions. The direction convention is not stated: signs appear to follow each test's scoring, so a positive value can mean worse (errors, time) or better (correct responses) performance.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: No inferential tests and no correction. Ranking 140 test variables from 15 small samples by size places chance extremes at the top of the list; 36 of the 41 rows with an absolute d of 0.50 or more rest on a single study (editors' count).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable at review level; who selected studies and extracted data, and whether either was done in duplicate, is not reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: Cohen's d per test variable, described as raw effect sizes (no small-sample correction), computed from means and SDs, F or t; for variables used in more than one study, the mean and SD of the study ds, with no weighting described and no confidence intervals, random-effects model or heterogeneity statistic (pp. 191, 193). Median effect size 0.35; U2 mean 0.58 (median 0.57; range 0.50–0.70) (pp. 193–194). Rows with five or more effect sizes (mean d; number of ds; SD): Trail Making A 0.19 (10; 0.51); Trail Making B 0.49 (9; 0.25); COWAT −0.19 (8; 0.34), listed again as −0.05 (9; 0.52); Stroop Color-Word Interference −0.11 (7; 0.67); WAIS-R Digit Symbol −0.49 (6; 0.46); Rey-Osterrieth delayed recall −0.45 (6; 0.35); WAIS-R Arithmetic −0.66 (5; 0.48); Rey-Osterrieth copy −0.47 (5; 0.47). The largest values, about 1 in absolute size, come from single studies (Speech Sounds Perception 1.09, favouring the cocaine group; grooved pegboard −1.07; BMAE oral fluency 1.04; MicroCog executive function −1.00). Editors' calculations: 93 of the 140 rows and 36 of the 41 rows with an absolute d of 0.50 or more rest on one study; a single-study d of 0.50 with 20 people per group has a 95% interval of about −0.13 to 1.13 (large-sample standard error); the Stroop Color row (2 ds, mean 0.49, SD 1.05) implies study values of about 1.23 and −0.25, that is, opposite directions.
analysis.covariates: None. Attribute variables (age, education, duration of use) were recorded but not analysed; the authors say a moderator analysis would need more studies using the same tests (pp. 191, 200).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: Table 2 does not show which studies contributed to each row, and the 15 included studies are identified only by asterisks in the reference list, so no summary value can be audited. The flow of records (found, screened, excluded) is not reported.
analysis.power: Not addressed. Cocaine samples of 16 to 61 people (median 30); most rows rest on one study of 16 to 61 people per group, so single-study values are imprecise (see the editors' interval above).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 15 small cross-sectional studies from 1987–2002, groups meeting criteria for cocaine abuse or dependence scored lower than control groups on many neuropsychological tests, mostly by small to moderate amounts: the median absolute d across 140 test variables was 0.35 and the average U2 0.58 (0.50 means no separation). The tests used most often gave d of about 0.1 to 0.7 with wide spread between studies (Trail Making B 0.49 across 9 effect sizes; Trail Making A 0.19 across 10; Stroop Color-Word interference −0.11 across 7). Values near 1 came from single small studies, the largest of them favouring the cocaine group. Differences also appeared on vocabulary and IQ measures that usually reflect prior ability, and the control groups' characteristics were not reported.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The aims and abstract attribute the differences to cocaine: the stated aim is to measure "deficits found as a result of cocaine use" (p. 191; also abstract, p. 189). The abstract headlines attention as most affected (0.40<d<1.10), but the upper bound is the Speech Sounds result, on which the cocaine group performed better (p. 194) and which the primary authors attributed to chance and to low control scores (p. 199); the Discussion itself notes that some executive and visual-memory effects were larger than the attention effects (p. 194). The abstract's minimal effects (d<0.30) for language and sensory-perceptual tests and its moderate-to-large (d>0.50) visual-memory effects do not match Table 2 (pp. 195–198), nor does the statement that the large attention effects rested on multiple studies (p. 199). The anterior cingulate and orbitofrontal account (abstract; p. 200) comes from other literature and is not tested, and implications for rehabilitation are drawn (p. 201). The limitations (pp. 200–201) concede variable abstinence, poorly documented amounts, mixed routes and concurrent alcohol abuse, but the conclusion is stated without these qualifications and without any comparison of premorbid ability.

timeline.event: Bolla, Cadet & London review of chronic cocaine use, cited by this review (p. 200) as concluding that long-term neurocognitive effects may be subtle and specific rather than generalized.

Bolla, Funderburk & Cadet compare people who used cocaine with people who used cocaine and alcohol; cited by this review (p. 201) as part of a mixed literature on combined effects, not among the 15 included studies.
This review: 15 studies, 140 test variables, median absolute d 0.35.
Spronk et al. comprehensive review of the cognitive effects of cocaine (to be appraised from its full text).
Frazer et al. systematic critical review of long-term cognitive effects of cocaine use (to be appraised from its full text).

López-Martín et al. (online 2025) meta-analysis of inhibition tasks, 20 studies published up to January 2024: g = 0.65 (0.28 to 1.03) for poorer inhibition in people with cocaine use disorder; it does not cite this review.

replication.where_it_stands: An early quantitative summary of a small literature, now exceeded in size by later reviews. Its numbers are descriptive transformations of 15 small cross-sectional studies, not pooled estimates, and should not be cited as such. The direction it describes (people meeting criteria for cocaine abuse or dependence score lower than controls on many tests, mostly by small to moderate amounts) agrees with the later inhibition meta-analysis (López-Martín et al., 2026), although the Stroop Color-Word interference result here (−0.11 across 7 effect sizes) is much smaller than that review's pooled estimate, which rests mostly on stop-signal and go/no-go tasks; cause, reversibility and clinical significance remain open. The primary studies in this review (for example Di Sclafani et al., 2002, on the cocaine list) are inside its summaries and must not be cited as independent support alongside it.

funding.funder: Not reported (the article has no funding or acknowledgement statement).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: All three authors at the University of Toronto (Life Sciences). The rationale for effect-size analysis and the overlap conversion cite the corresponding author's earlier papers (Zakzanis, 1998, 2001; pp. 190–191). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A properly weighted random-effects (or individual-participant) meta-analysis of the now larger literature, using harmonized cognitive domains and checked effect sizes, restricted to control groups matched on education and premorbid IQ, separating recent from prolonged abstinence and adjusting for alcohol; and, for cause, prospective cohorts with cognitive testing before regular cocaine use begins, or co-twin and sibling designs.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (DSM-III-R or DSM-IV cocaine abuse or dependence), comparison (matched healthy controls), outcomes (neuropsychological test variables) and four research questions are stated (pp. 191–192).
Only cross-sectional comparisons with matched controls were eligible; the choice is not explained, and longitudinal or within-person studies are not discussed.

Two databases with keywords listed; published English-language articles only, without justification of the language limit; no reference-list, grey-literature or registry search; search date not reported. The 1987 start is justified (DSM-III-R). Judged no under AMSTAR 2 item 4 as written, as for batch 3 cards; the senior author decides the project's reading (decision p-amstar2-item4).
Who selected studies, and whether in duplicate, is not reported.
Who extracted data, and whether in duplicate or checked, is not reported.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: No list of excluded studies and no counts of records screened or excluded.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Included studies are identified only by asterisks in the reference list; Table 1 summarizes them in aggregate (medians, ranges) with no per-study description of samples, diagnoses, abstinence, tests or controls.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No assessment of the quality or risk of bias of the included studies.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: Study ds were averaged as simple means and SDs, with no weighting described, no confidence intervals, no random-effects model and no heterogeneity statistic; d without small-sample correction; correlated variables from the same samples are treated as separate entries, and the same fluency data appear in more than one row.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No risk-of-bias assessment, so no analysis of its impact.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Generic limitations are discussed (abstinence, amounts, route, alcohol), and alcohol is named as a possible partial explanation (pp. 200–201), but no study-level bias was assessed, premorbid differences are not considered, and the conclusions remain causal and unqualified.
SDs of study ds are reported (up to 1.05) but heterogeneity is neither investigated nor explained; a moderator analysis is judged not possible (p. 200).

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: No funding or conflict-of-interest statement for the review.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Seven critical items fail (2, 4, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15), so confidence is critically low by the AMSTAR 2 rule. The review is open that most rows are single-study effect sizes, and it predates current reporting standards, but its numbers are descriptive transformations of 15 small cross-sectional studies: no weighting or intervals, no appraisal of the studies, unknown completeness of the search, and duplicated and sign-ambiguous rows. It may be cited for: the size of group differences on particular multi-study tests in the 1987–2002 literature (for example Trail Making B 0.49 across 9 effect sizes, Trail Making A 0.19 across 10, Stroop Color-Word interference −0.11 across 7), the observation that the largest differences came from single small studies, and the authors' own interpretation. It may not be cited for: a pooled estimate of cognitive impairment caused by cocaine, the abstract's attention range of 0.40 to 1.10, effects of abstinence or recovery, or clinical significance.

key_findings.finding: Fifteen studies met the inclusion criteria; test results came from 481 people meeting criteria for cocaine abuse or dependence and 586 healthy control participants. Where a primary study tested people more than once, only the first occasion was used, to avoid practice effects.
key_findings.note: The control total does not match Table 1 (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Search and eligibility: PsycINFO and Medline, published English-language articles; inclusion required publication between 1987 and 2002, statistics convertible to d, DSM-III-R or DSM-IV criteria for cocaine abuse or dependence, and a matched healthy control group; samples with concurrent alcohol abuse (not dependence) were allowed. No search date, record flow, duplicate selection or extraction, or quality appraisal is reported.
key_findings.locator: Method › Literature Search, 1st paragraph; Criteria for Inclusion, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Cocaine groups (Table 1): study mean ages median 34 (range 26–40); men median 95% (mean 87%, range 53–100); education mean 12.2 years (range of study means 5.4–14.1); duration of use reported by 10 studies (median 77.3 months, range 8.5–169.0); abstinence at testing reported by 11 studies (median 23.6 days, mean 128.7, SD 317.0, range 0–1075.5). Control groups are described only by sample size (median 27, range 16–138).

Across all test variables the median effect size was 0.35, and the mean U2 0.58 (median 0.57, range 0.50–0.70); the authors read a U2 of 0.70 as 30% of control scores overlapping with those of the cocaine group. By the editors' count, Table 2 lists 140 test variables, 93 of them from a single study.
key_findings.note: Editors' recomputation from the 140 rows of Table 2: median absolute d about 0.34 and mean U2 0.57, close to the printed values. The printed median must be of absolute values, since the signed values have a median of about −0.27. U2 of 0.50 means no separation of the groups; every printed U2 equals Φ(|d|/2) within 0.01, so it adds nothing beyond d.

key_findings.finding: Test variables with five or more effect sizes (mean d; number of ds; SD of the ds; cocaine vs control participants): Trail Making A 0.19 (10; 0.51; 330 vs 374); Trail Making B 0.49 (9; 0.25; 300 vs 344); COWAT −0.19 (8; 0.34; 265 vs 336), listed again as −0.05 (9; 0.52; 285 vs 356); Stroop Color-Word Interference −0.11 (7; 0.67; 243 vs 308); WAIS-R Digit Symbol −0.49 (6; 0.46; 170 vs 145); Rey-Osterrieth delayed recall −0.45 (6; 0.35; 205 vs 244); WAIS-R Arithmetic −0.66 (5; 0.48; 146 vs 100); Rey-Osterrieth copy −0.47 (5; 0.47; 168 vs 217).
key_findings.locator: Table 2: WAIS-R Arithmetic p. 195; Trail Making B, WAIS-R Digit Symbol and the two ROCF rows p. 196; Trail Making A, the first COWAT row and Stroop Color-Word p. 197; the second COWAT row p. 198
key_findings.note: The paper does not state its sign convention. Assuming the usual scoring of these tests (time for Trail Making, correct responses or scaled scores for the others), all eight point to poorer performance in the cocaine groups.

key_findings.finding: The largest values all come from one or two small studies: Speech Sounds Perception Test 1.09 (30 vs 30), on which the cocaine group performed better, a result the primary authors attributed to chance and to controls scoring low against norms; grooved pegboard, hand unspecified, −1.07 (20 vs 29); BMAE oral fluency 1.04 (20 vs 20); MicroCog executive function −1.00 and spatial processing −0.96 (20 vs 29); WAIS-R Vocabulary −0.95 (19 vs 16); WAIS-R Picture Arrangement −0.90 (2 studies; 49 vs 46); Benton Visual Retention Test errors 0.82 (38 vs 54); Booklet Categories Test errors 0.77 (2 studies; 58 vs 74).

Memory: the larger differences come from single studies (RAVLT trials 1–5 total −0.76, 16 vs 21; CVLT short-delay cued recall −0.71; RMT picture recall −0.69) or the Benton Visual Retention Test (number correct −0.71, 2 studies); measures used in three or more studies were smaller: CVLT long-delay free recall −0.30 (4), CVLT short-delay free recall −0.36 (3), WMS Logical Memory immediate −0.39 and delayed −0.03 (3 each), WMS-R Logical Memory immediate −0.16 and delayed −0.19 (3 each), Rey-Osterrieth delayed recall −0.45 (6); the WMS and WMS-R visual reproduction rows range from −0.01 to −0.43.

Executive tests diverge: Booklet Categories Test errors 0.77 (2 studies) and MicroCog executive function −1.00 (1 study) are large, but every Wisconsin Card Sorting Test variable is small (perseverative errors 0.23, 2 studies; categories −0.17, 4; perseverative responses 0.09, 3; number of errors −0.07, 3; failure to maintain set −0.06, 3; number correct −0.03 and trials to first category 0.00, 1 each). The authors explain the contrast by the Category Test's greater difficulty, citing one primary study that gave both tests.

Motor and sensory tests were mostly small (finger tapping dominant hand 0.01 and non-dominant −0.24, 2 studies each; grooved pegboard dominant 0.24, SD 0.74, and non-dominant 0.01, 4 studies each; finger gnosis 0.17 and 0.29), with two single-study exceptions: grooved pegboard, hand unspecified, −1.07, and finger tapping, right, −0.61 (30 vs 21).

Differences also appear on measures usually taken to reflect prior verbal ability or schooling: WAIS-R Vocabulary −0.95 (19 vs 16), WAIS Full Scale IQ −0.66 and Verbal IQ −0.62 (61 vs 63), Shipley-Hartford vocabulary −0.54 (40 vs 40), WRMT Word Attack −0.41 (38 vs 54), each from one study; WAIS-R Full Scale IQ, from three studies, was −0.08 (110 vs 188).
key_findings.note: Reading these as signs of pre-existing group differences is the editors' interpretation; the review does not discuss them or report the control groups' education or IQ.

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: different tests across studies, preventing a full meta-analysis and a moderator analysis; abstinence from 0 to 1075.5 days, raising the question of acute versus abstinence effects; widely different and often unreported amounts and durations of use; mixed routes (mostly smoked freebase or crack, some intravenous or intranasal); concurrent caffeine, nicotine and alcohol use, with alcohol abuse allowed, so that the differences could be at least partly due to alcohol.

The authors conclude that the analysis provides effect-size evidence of attentional deficits and of impairments in more complex executive abstraction abilities, place them in the anterior cingulate and orbitofrontal cortex on the basis of earlier imaging and neurochemical literature, and recommend cognitive strategies aimed at attention and executive abilities in treatment programmes.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and the Results give 586 control participants, but Table 1 gives a mean control-sample size of 36 across 15 studies, while the cocaine total of 481 agrees with its Table 1 mean of 32. By the editors' calculation the control mean totals about 540 (a mean of up to 36.5 would give at most 548).
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the two control figures is wrong by about 40 to 46 people; cite the number of controls as printed (586) with this discrepancy noted.

reporting_issues.issue: COWAT appears twice in Table 2: 8 effect sizes, mean −0.19 (SD 0.34; 265 vs 336) on p. 197, and 9 effect sizes, mean −0.05 (SD 0.52; 285 vs 356) on p. 198. Editors' calculation: adding the BMAE oral fluency value (1.04; 20 vs 20; p. 195) to the 8-effect row reproduces the 9-effect row exactly (mean −0.053, SD 0.519 with n−1, and 20 more people in each group).
reporting_issues.consequence: The same data appear in two or three rows, with two different summary values for the most-used fluency test; the fluency result depends on whether a single-study value of opposite sign (+1.04) is pooled with the COWAT studies. The 8-effect row appears to be the summary of the COWAT studies alone.

reporting_issues.issue: The sign convention for d is not stated. Signs appear to follow each test's scoring (positive for errors or time where the cocaine group scored higher, negative for correct-response scores where it scored lower), so a positive d can mean worse or better performance. The text identifies only the Speech Sounds result (1.09) as favouring the cocaine group, but several positive values are on tests usually scored so that higher is better (BMAE oral fluency 1.04, Hooper Visual Organization 0.40, RAVLT total 0.37, WAIS-R Verbal IQ 0.36, RAVLT delayed recall 0.35) and are not discussed, although the introduction notes that some primary studies found better verbal fluency in people using cocaine (p. 190). The ranking and the median use absolute values.
reporting_issues.consequence: For these rows a reader cannot tell from the paper whether the cocaine group did worse or better; claims should not use them as deficits, and the ranking by size mixes deficits with possible advantages.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract states minimal effects (d<0.30) for verbal fluency, other language functions and sensory-perceptual tests, but Table 2 lists BMAE oral fluency 1.04, fingertip number writing (non-dominant hand) 0.46, BMAE reading comprehension −0.43, WRMT Word Attack −0.41, Boston Naming −0.35 and BMAE aural comprehension 0.32. It also states moderate to large effects (d>0.50) for visual and working memory, whereas the WMS and WMS-R visual reproduction rows range from −0.01 to −0.43, Rey-Osterrieth delayed recall is −0.45 and Backward Digit Span −0.46.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's domain summary is selective; any statement about a cognitive domain must be checked against the individual rows of Table 2.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion states that most of the other relatively large attention effects were based on multiple studies (p. 199), but of the 14 attention measures the Results place above the median (pp. 193–194), 9 rest on a single study in Table 2 (editors' count). The multi-study ones are WAIS-R Arithmetic (5), WAIS-R Digit Symbol (6), Trail Making B (9), Symbol Digit written (3) and Stroop Color (2), and the Stroop Color mean of 0.49 has an SD of 1.05.
reporting_issues.consequence: The attention profile that the abstract headlines rests mostly on single small studies. Among replicated attention measures the means range from about 0.5 to 0.7, while Trail Making A (10 effect sizes) is 0.19 and Stroop Color-Word interference (7) is −0.11.

reporting_issues.issue: Text and table disagree on two motor results: the grooved pegboard with hand unspecified (d=−1.07) is called the third largest effect (p. 194) but is second in Table 2's rank order (p. 195); and the Discussion says motor tests showed minimal effects with only one exception (p. 194), while Table 2 also lists finger tapping, right, at −0.61 (one study, 30 vs 21).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the motor summary understates the scatter of single-study motor results.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion states that studies of people with concurrent alcohol dependence were excluded (p. 201), but the included studies (asterisked in the references) include Robinson, Heaton & O'Malley (1999), whose title compares people with and without alcohol dependence, and Di Sclafani et al. (2002), whose title names a group dependent on crack cocaine and alcohol; the review does not say which subgroups it used.
reporting_issues.consequence: If alcohol-dependent groups entered any row, the attribution of differences to cocaine is further confounded; the primary studies are needed to check.

reporting_issues.issue: One included study, Goldstein et al. on orbitofrontal function and response inhibition, has no year in the reference list, so the 1987–2002 criterion cannot be checked from this paper (editors' note: López-Martín et al., 2026, list the same title with the year 2001).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; with no table linking studies to rows, the included-study list cannot be fully verified from the review alone.

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record, J Clin Exp Neuropsychol 27(2):189–204; Taylor & Francis download with an unnumbered publisher's cover page): all 17 PDF pages read (cover page, then printed pp. 189–204 as PDF pp. 2–17); Tables 1 and 2 and every number on this card checked on pages rendered at 150 dpi; no figures; no supplement. Anchors give the printed page.
